rationale:
Today's slate stays inside the GLP-1 focus and follows the 11-17 growth playbook.

**Long video.** Queue items #1–3 have shipped (Nausea Foods on 11-17, Mounjaro vs Zepbound on 11-18, Weight Loss in the Trials on 11-19), so today is #4: Orforglipron (Foundayo) Pill: What to Expect. It is an approved-drug, search-demand video, which is also priority action #1 in the analytics. Foundayo already gains about 30 minutes a day. The radar's strongest signal (momentum 88) is the TGA approval on 11-16 and the Health Canada approval on 11-18, both in high-ad-rate markets. That makes this the fast-turn version of the EloraTZP model, but on a settled body of evidence (the US label plus the Phase 3 ATTAIN-1 trial in NEJM) instead of breaking news. It is a re-render of the verified 11-11 script, which was held for audio, with its known faults fixed. The Canada and Australia news goes in packaging and the description only, so the verified narration stays unchanged and evergreen.

**Shorts.** All 3 are felt-symptom or practical moments, and every working title puts the drug first:
- **S1 (08:00):** a bruise at the tirzepatide injection site, a visible "Is this normal?" pen moment. Its post notes name the Pen how-to video as the related-video target.
- **S2 (13:00):** a spin-off of L1 and a gentle myth-flip ("a pill means no nausea?"). It carries the timely Foundayo hook in Short form.
- **S3 (20:00):** the holiday-table slot. Leftovers is the one holiday moment not yet covered (full after 3 bites, heartburn, drinks, the morning after, flying and greasy meals are all done). Its target is the Thanksgiving long video.

**Carousel.** The quota asks for one, so it reuses only the verified, shipped 11-19 pen-disposal Short as a TikTok photo post. It must fix that Short's two known QA faults: placeholder source dates and the validation hook in the caption.

**Mix.**
- **Emerging:** L1 and S2 (the Foundayo approvals).
- **Evergreen with a timely hook:** S1 and C1.
- **Peaking seasonal:** S3.
- **Myth-busting:** S2.

**Pillars.** No pillar is used more than twice: research ×1, myths ×1, get-the-most ×1, life-on-glp1 ×2. Body systems are spread out: one drug overview, one skin/injection, one GI, one food storage and one device.

**Skipped.** Nothing marked reject was used. Caution topics are skipped today:
- NAION is already covered by the 11-10 Short and the Serious Risks chapter.
- Serious Risks stays in the queue as #6.
- Not-working, teens, binge eating and retatrutide are left out.

pieces.topic: Starting orforglipron (Foundayo), the once-daily GLP-1 pill approved for chronic weight management: what to expect in the first weeks and months, from the US prescribing information and Medication Guide (playbook queue #4: fixed re-render of the verified, held 11-11 script)
pieces.angle: Same locked script and US label scope. Packaging change: description paragraph 1 is the safety block. The regulator line, placed after it, reads: 'Health Canada (13 Nov 2026) and Australia's TGA (16 Nov 2026) have also approved Foundayo. This video explains the US label; indications and details can differ, so check your local leaflet.' Include it only after you've confirmed both dates on the regulators' own pages (Health Canada Notice of Compliance or Drug Product Database; TGA ARTG entry). Otherwise drop the line. NAION: quote the live PI if it's printed there; if not, say 'In November 2026 the FDA asked all GLP-1 medicine labels to add a warning about a rare eye condition called NAION' and credit the 9 Nov 2026 Drug Safety Communication.
pieces.why: Queue #4 and an approved-drug search-demand video. The existing Foundayo video gains about 30 minutes a day from 'foundayo' searches, and the Canadian and Australian approvals in the last 72 hours add fresh demand in high-ad-rate markets. The body rests on the label plus the Phase 3 ATTAIN-1 trial, so it's verifiable in depth. | fact-check: I'm approving the re-render of the verified 11-11 script. Narration stays locked to the US label (FDA approved 1 Apr 2026; PI at uspl.lilly.com/foundayo/foundayo.html). I checked the claims that sit outside the narration. (1) The FDA Drug Safety Communication on NAION for the whole GLP-1 class is real and dated 9 Nov 2026. It requires a new Warnings and Precautions section on every GLP-1 RA label. Check whether the live Foundayo PI already prints NAION. If it does, quote the label. If it doesn't, credit the FDA communication. Never call it 'new'. (2) Health Canada's date is wrong. Diabetes Toolbox (Canada) says Health Canada approved Foundayo on 13 Nov 2026. 18 Nov is when the news coverage ran. (3) The TGA date checks out: Foundayo went on the ARTG on 16 Nov 2026 (RACGP newsGP, mivision). The Canadian and Australian approvals cover weight management and type 2 diabetes, and Canada's product notice says 'capsules'. That makes the 'check your local leaflet' line necessary. (4) The description order breaks our rule. Safety block (scoped don't-stop line plus disclaimer) goes first, then the regulator note, then the quick answer and 2–3 sources. The publisher's Watch next line goes after the safety block, never as line 1. Line 1 stays empty. Keep it to 1,250 characters or fewer and end on '…whether it's right for you.' (5) The video has no dose steps, so the thumbnail 'FIRST MONTH?' must not suggest a week-by-week dose schedule. A pill bottle with a calm character is fine. Fix the known faults first: masking 0.02 or lower on the final file, every cut re-timed from the final word timestamps to within 0.5 s, Dana's skin and hair locked. Regenerate the broken audio scene and check its speech-to-text against the script word for word.

pieces.topic: A bruise where you injected tirzepatide: what the label counts as an injection-site reaction, why rotating sites is advised in the Instructions for Use, and when a mark needs a call
pieces.angle:
08:00 calm 'Is this normal?' visible pen moment. Follow the task's length arm and hook archetype.
- Sentence 1 (14 words or fewer): 'Tirzepatide shot left a small bruise? Here's what the label counts.' Scene 1's on-screen text matches it.
- By 6 s, the relief fact goes in the same line, with no standalone validation sentence: bruising is one of the terms the Zepbound label groups under injection-site reactions, 6–8% by dose vs about 2% on placebo. Copy the term list exactly from the label (PI rev. 28 Aug 2026, section 6.1).
- Credit 'change (rotate) your injection site each week' only to the single-dose pen IFU at its own URL, quoted only if it loads.
- Untagged red flags: spreading redness, warmth, pus or fever means call your prescriber.

pieces.topic: Orforglipron (Foundayo) is a pill, so why can it still cause nausea? GI side effects on the label vs placebo
pieces.angle: Sentence 1 as planned. By 6 s: 'The US label lists nausea as a common side effect: X% on orforglipron vs Y% on placebo.' (Use L1's verified numbers, arms and population.) Then a plain sentence from label 12.1: 'Like the injected GLP-1 medicines, orforglipron is a GLP-1 receptor agonist. It works on the same receptor, just in pill form.' Drop 'how you take it doesn't change what it does' and any explanation of what causes the nausea. Timing goes in label wording as a trial pattern. Keep the 2 untagged tips, the severe-stomach-pain emergency card, the scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line.
pieces.working_title: Orforglipron (Foundayo): Why Can a Pill Cause Nausea? #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1: it rides the fresh Canadian and Australian approvals (the radar suggested this exact question), stays a felt-symptom Short, and drives viewers to the Foundayo long video. | fact-check: The topic is fine, but one planned sentence overstates the science. 'How you take it doesn't change what it does' isn't label wording and isn't strictly true. Orforglipron is a non-peptide small molecule, and its absorption and dosing differ from the injectable peptides. Section 12.1 supports only that it is a GLP-1 receptor agonist. Nothing in the label says nausea comes from receptor action and not from the route, so don't imply that cause either. The nausea rate per arm vs placebo must match L1's verified script exactly, including the drug, the arms, the ATTAIN-1 population and 72 weeks. Timing goes in the label's words ('mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time', if that is the Foundayo wording) and is framed as a trial pattern. The severe-stomach-pain line follows the label's pancreatitis wording and keeps 'right away'. The related-video target should be the Side Effects video until L1 is live.

pieces.topic: Thanksgiving leftovers when tirzepatide means smaller portions: how long leftovers keep in the fridge and freezer, per US food-safety guidance
pieces.angle:
20:00 holiday-table Short. Follow the task's length arm and hook archetype.
- Sentence 1 (14 words or fewer): 'On tirzepatide, Thanksgiving leftovers may outlast your appetite. Here's how long they keep.' Scene 1's on-screen text matches it.
- By 6 s: refrigerate within 2 hours, and eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days (FoodSafety.gov/USDA, copied exactly with the page's live date).
- Second fact: freeze portions for longer storage, worded only as the USDA page prints it.
- Separate label sentence, no 'so': tirzepatide reduces appetite and food intake.
- Untagged tips, 2 at most: box small portions straight away; label containers with the date.
- No guilt, no 'bad' foods, no calorie talk.
- Safety line: vomiting or diarrhoea you can't keep up with means contact your prescriber (the label links fluid loss to kidney problems). Then the scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and a loop line.
- Note that rules elsewhere may differ, but use no extra country sources.
- Post note: the related-video target is the Thanksgiving long video.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide and Thanksgiving Leftovers: How Long Do They Keep? #shorts
pieces.why: The holiday-table slot runs through 11-27, and search peaks the week of Nov 23. Leftovers is the only holiday moment from the playbook list not yet made, and it's a practical moment that feeds the Thanksgiving long video.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) months 2–6: what to expect after the first month, organised by experience (appetite, how stomach side effects tend to change, the shape of average weight change, hair shedding, the oral-contraceptive note around dose increases, injection-site reactions), using only the US Zepbound label (rev. 28 Aug 2026) and SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM 2022). Playbook queue #5, the sequel to First Month.
pieces.angle: Tirzepatide after the first month: what usually changes, organised by experience and drawn only from the US Zepbound label (rev. 28 Aug 2026), SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM 2022) and the Mounjaro label (rev. 27 Aug 2026) for any shared statement. If the Mounjaro label isn't used, retitle to 'Tirzepatide (Zepbound) After Month 1: What to Expect' and leave Mounjaro out of all packaging. Use 'months two to six' only as the viewer's frame, and never tie an effect to a specific month. Line for the 15 s payoff: 'stomach side effects happened mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time, and in SURMOUNT-1 average weight kept going down for many months.' Second payoff: nausea as a by-dose range versus placebo (no mg figures spoken or shown), with the label's pooled-trial population copied exactly from section 6.1. Keep every other chapter, safety line and structural rule as briefed: appetite in label wording, the hedged 'food noise' framing, the 72-week SURMOUNT-1 average with its full population ('averages, not predictions'), hair 5.4% vs 0.9% (women 7.1%, men 0.5%), and oral hormonal contraceptives 'for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase' with no increase schedule. Injection-site reactions are 6–8% by dose vs about 2% on placebo, with the rotation tip credited to the IFU or paraphrased from the label. Protein comes with a kidney caveat, and strength training 2+ days a week is marked 'recommended'. Include the diabetes-plus-insulin/sulfonylurea low-blood-sugar line and the severe-stomach-pain emergency line, followed by the scoped don't-switch/stop/change line. No dose numbers, and the 'Not personal advice' and prescriber lines are both spoken and shown on screen.
pieces.why:
This is the next ready item in the playbook queue (#5) and a search-demand timeline that completes the First Month series. Every fact comes from the label and SURMOUNT-1, already verified, so it should pass the fact-check first time. Confirm the 11-16 plan never went live before rendering. | fact-check: Good evergreen sequel to First Month. It's on-pillar and has real search demand, and the brief already fixes most of the known failure modes: label wording for GI effects, the hair-loss figures, the injection-site figures, oral contraceptives only, the low-blood-sugar scope, the emergency line and no dosing calendar. Four things need fixing before scripting.
(1) Mounjaro scope: the working title and the topic both name Mounjaro, but the only sources listed are the Zepbound label and SURMOUNT-1. The house rule says a Mounjaro keyword needs Mounjaro's own label (PI rev 27 Aug 2026). Either cite it for the shared sections (contraceptive interaction, GI, injection site) or drop 'Mounjaro' from the title and hashtags. Keep in mind that Mounjaro's figures come from type 2 diabetes trials, so never mix its numbers with Zepbound's.
(2) Internal conflict: the brief asks for 'one pooled nausea rate per dose' but also 'no dose numbers'. Give the rate as a by-dose range ('about X to Y in 100, depending on dose, versus about Z in 100 on placebo'), copied from Zepbound section 6.1, and name the label's pooled-trial population exactly as printed. Don't call it SURMOUNT-1 only, and don't add or drop 'with or without type 2 diabetes'. Read the pool definition in the label and don't assume it.
(3) Timeline framing: neither source reports outcomes by month 2, 3 and so on. 'Months 2–6' can be the viewer's frame, but the script must not attach any effect to a specific month. Hair shedding has no timing in the label, and weight change is described over 72 weeks. The 15 s payoff should say 'in SURMOUNT-1', not 'in the trials', and the wording should be 'average weight kept going down for many months', with no plateau week read off the graph.
(4) The contraceptive chapter should say 'after starting and after each dose increase' without saying how often increases happen. That keeps any titration calendar out.
Other notes: the brief's spoken closing line is fine, but the description watch-next line is added by the publisher (target: Side Effects). Mention it only in post notes and don't type it into the description.
